exemplars.title: Explaining Research Findings with Confidence
exemplars.teaching_need: Undergraduates often struggle to turn research evidence into a clear, accurate explanation for non-specialists—mixing findings with interpretation, overstating certainty, and improving work without developing evaluative judgement.
exemplars.intended_capability: Interpret and communicate a research finding accurately and appropriately for a non-specialist audience, and improve an explanation through comparison, self-diagnosis and reasoned revision.
exemplars.summary: A 90-minute Learning Journey in which learners interpret a self-contained research study, write a first explanation, compare contrasting examples against quality criteria, diagnose and revise their own work, then account for what changed—supported by a Learning Journal that preserves learner-authored artefacts.
exemplars.primary_pattern: Evaluative judgement through comparison, self-diagnosis and revision (draft → judge → revise)
supporting_patterns: Initial independent performance before worked examples or detailed evaluative guidance
Comparison of contrasting explanations against explicit quality criteria
Self-assessment and diagnosis of own work
Iterative improvement of a retained first attempt
Reflection on changes made and why they matter
Learning Journal preserving learner-authored work across the sequence
learning_sequence: Overview — orientation to the journey and expectations
Interpret the research evidence (Interactive) — build understanding of a self-contained illustrative study
Write your first explanation (Assessment Pack) — independent explanation for a non-specialist reader, retained as a baseline
Compare explanations and judge their quality (Interactive) — contrast examples and practise comparative judgement
Diagnose your explanation (Assessment Pack) — apply criteria to your own first attempt
Revise your explanation (Assessment Pack) — improve the retained baseline in light of diagnosis
Explain what changed and why (Expository) — account for revisions and their significance
Learning Journal — preserve and revisit learner-authored work across the journey
exemplars.transferable_principle: When the goal is evaluative judgement rather than a single correct answer, have learners produce an independent attempt first, then use comparison against explicit criteria, self-diagnosis and revision—preserving the original work so improvement can be reasoned about. The subject matter and exact activities can change; the draft–judge–revise logic travels.

exemplars.title: The Decision That Went Wrong
exemplars.teaching_need: Learners often struggle to make a defensible institutional recommendation when evidence is incomplete, conflicting and consequential—mistaking early promising results for settled proof, overlooking stakeholder impacts, or treating uncertainty as a reason to avoid judgement.
exemplars.intended_capability: Interpret conflicting quantitative and qualitative evidence in a developing institutional case, weigh stakeholder perspectives and trade-offs, and reach a justified recommendation under genuine uncertainty.
exemplars.summary: A 90-minute Learning Journey set in a fictional UK university considering an AI-assisted student support system. Learners meet early pilot evidence, examine it more carefully, encounter later conflicting findings and stakeholder perspectives, then produce a committee recommendation that remains open to more than one defensible outcome.
exemplars.primary_pattern: Evidence-informed decision-making under uncertainty through progressive disclosure of conflicting evidence
supporting_patterns: Critical interpretation of quantitative and qualitative evaluation findings
Attention to stakeholder perspectives and consequences
Reasoning under uncertainty with genuine ambiguity preserved
Justified recommendation with opportunity to reconsider earlier judgement
learning_sequence: Overview — orientation to the institutional case and expectations
The Promising Pilot (Interactive) — make sense of early evaluation evidence and form an initial case
Reading the Evidence Carefully (Expository) — examine what the figures and records can and cannot support
When the Evidence Changes (Interactive) — weigh later findings, benefits, concerns and reconsider earlier judgement
The People Behind the Decision (Interactive) — consider stakeholder consequences and what the evidence can support
The Committee Recommendation (Assessment Pack) — choose among options and justify a recommendation under uncertainty
exemplars.transferable_principle: When there is no single unambiguously correct decision, develop judgement by revealing evidence progressively, distinguishing observation from interpretation, bringing stakeholder consequences into view, and requiring a justified recommendation that can survive new or conflicting information. The institutional AI scenario is the vehicle, not the transferable core.
